question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14151706/assets/36008a9155a01a07136cee263ce0a89239719227541536e8c2f8ea358d43e6df.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
question.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\cancel{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
